blocks.c: Not gracefully. I went across a dark terrazzo floor with my arms out like a man in a comedy, hit the corner of the desk with my hip hard enough to bruise for a week, found the elevator by the light of my phone, got in, and hit every button on the panel at once.
The doors closed. The car went up.
The doors opened on B2 of the actual Merridew Tower, with the chiller howling and the fluorescent tube by the pump room doing the flicker it has done since November.
I sat down on the floor of the freight car and shook for a while.
Then I opened the log book.

I wrote for forty minutes. Everything: the key, the tag, the button, the eleven seconds, the ficus, the visitor book, my own name in my own hand, the time I wrote in the OUT column, the lights, the voice.
When I finished, my hands had stopped shaking and something else had happened, which is that I had noticed a detail I had not noticed while it was happening.
The visitor book had columns for IN and OUT.
Which means people are expected to leave.

Which means the entire hundreds-of-names, nobody-signed-out thing is not the building being a trap. It is the building keeping score. There is a difference and the difference is enormous, and the difference is the reason I am still here.
I turned to the back of my log book to write that down where I would see it.
There was already something written on the last page.
It was in block capitals, in a pen that was not mine, and it was dated that night.
GOOD. YOU SIGNED OUT. THAT MAKES YOU THE FIRST IN ELEVEN YEARS. COME BACK TOMORROW AND BRING THE 1994 BOOK. — W.A.
